name: Dichanthelium

project_scope.selection_mode: existing-species genus FINISH/ENRICH; no new admissions

project_scope.note: These four are the installed canonical project concepts, NOT a comprehensive county-native Dichanthelium checklist.

look_here_first: TWO SEASONS, TWO LOOKS: search at the base for winter/spring rosette leaves; then inspect spring panicle, autumn leafy branches, collar/TRUE ligule hairs and measured mature spikelets. An airy panicle alone does not distinguish the species.

recognition.where_to_look_first: Identify the basal rosette (if present) and whether the plant has long spring culms versus densely leafy autumn branches. Spread a stem leaf to see if its base is rounded or cordate; inspect TRUE ligule at the blade–sheath junction, sheath hair bases and mature spikelets with a millimeter scale.
priority: winter rosette versus no obvious rosette
true ligule length and form, not blade-base cilia
sheath hair type and raised hair bases
mature individual spikelet length and outline

comparison_lesson.memory_rule: ROSETTE? LEAF BASE? COLLAR HAIRS? CALIBRATED SPIKELET? Check all four before naming a species.
quick_split: D. lindheimeri — tiny blunt spikelets (~1.3–1.6 mm), comparatively hairless yellow-green blades/sheaths, basal margin cilia and several-mm ligular hairs; compare fall branching.
D. commutatum — often broader, sometimes heart-based stem leaves; true ligule minute or absent; comparatively few-flowered open panicle; spikelets ~2.1–3.2 mm.
D. oligosanthes — conspicuous rosette phase with larger (~2.9–4 mm) spikelets; usually a more noticeable hair ligule and variably pustulate hairy sheaths.
D. pedicellatum — thin narrow leaves (often ~1.3–5.5 mm), short collar hair fringe (~0.25–0.5 mm), larger (~3–3.5 mm) spikelets.
comparison_lesson.guardrail: Size ranges and hairiness OVERLAP; measure several mature spikelets from an intact plant. Fall branches differ from spring culms. Never identify an entire genus or species from the single existing image without verification.
comparison_lesson.taxonomy_caution: The project's D. lindheimeri is also treated in some sources as D. acuminatum var. lindheimeri; do not duplicate. Scribnerianum may be treated under D. oligosanthes in older literature; do not merge or split source concepts without taxon review.

comparison_matrix.title: Dichanthelium — four installed rosette-grass concepts
rows: Sheath backs often nearly smooth; margins hairy
Often nearly glabrous except basal marginal cilia
Blade upper surface minutely hairy; lower often smoother
Rosette and leafy, branched autumn shoots
Winter rosette conspicuous in suitable season
Narrow thin leaves + tiny collar fringe + mature spikelet

what_to_teach_crew: One plant can look like two different grasses in spring and late fall—follow the stem all the way to its base.
Photograph the leaf blade and sheath from the same stem; pull the blade gently to expose the true ligule.
Don't confuse long hairs ON THE BLADE BASE with the TRUE ligule at the collar.
Always photograph three mature spikelets beside a millimeter ruler; a grass-specific hand lens/macro is essential.
Store first-pass unknowns as 'Dichanthelium sp.' rather than inventing a species call.
visual_needs: One whole rosette-to-panicle image per species, same plant and date.
Fresh true ligule/collar macro and upper/lower blade surface macro for all four species.
Scale-calibrated mature spikelets and individual glumes for all four; large (~3 mm) versus tiny (~1.5 mm) contrast.
Linked spring and autumn photos from the same plant (especially D. lindheimeri and D. oligosanthes).
Inspect the actual existing four photo binaries and place arrows ONLY on structures physically visible; no arbitrary image coordinates.
